items.prompt: In graph theory, what is the term for the points that are joined together by edges?

options.label: Faces
Loops
Vertices
Weights

rubric: Vertices (nodes) are the points of a graph that edges connect.
Faces are regions in planar drawings; loops and weights are other concepts.

items.prompt: What is the degree of a vertex in a simple undirected graph?

options.label: The number of vertices in the graph
The number of edges incident to it
The number of vertices at distance two from it
The length of the longest cycle through it

rubric: Degree counts the edges meeting at the vertex.
Other options confuse degree with order or cycle length.

items.prompt: What is a cycle in a graph?

options.label: A trail that uses every edge of the graph exactly once
A walk that starts and ends at the same vertex, repeats allowed
A set of vertices with no edges between any two of them
A closed path that repeats no vertex except the start and end

rubric: A cycle is a closed path with no repeated vertices apart from start/end.
Visiting every edge once describes an Euler trail; the last option describes an independent set.

items.prompt: Which statement defines a tree?

options.label: A connected graph with no cycles
A graph in which every vertex has degree two
A graph with exactly one vertex of degree one
A graph with no edges

rubric: A tree is connected and acyclic.
Degree-two graphs are cycles or unions of them; a tree has at least two leaves.

items.prompt: In a proper vertex coloring, which rule must hold?

options.label: Adjacent vertices get the same color
Every vertex gets a different color
Adjacent vertices get different colors
Each color is used equally often

rubric: Proper coloring forbids the same color on adjacent vertices.
Distinct colors for all vertices is not required.

items.prompt: Which of the following are standard ways to represent a graph? Select all that apply.

options.label: Adjacency list
Adjacency matrix
Degree sequence listing only each vertex's number of neighbours
Vertex coloring table

items.prompt: A student draws a graph of friendships in a class. Each person is a dot, and a line joins two dots if those people are friends. Friendship is mutual. Which type of graph is this?

options.label: An undirected graph
A weighted directed graph
A directed graph
A bipartite tree

rubric: Mutual relationships give undirected edges.
Directed graphs are for one-way relationships.

items.prompt: A graph has 5 vertices with degrees 2, 2, 3, 3 and 2. How many edges does it have?
rubric: Handshake lemma: degree sum 12 equals twice the edges, so 6.
12 forgets to halve the sum.

items.prompt: Why does every tree with n vertices have exactly n-1 edges?

options.label: Each vertex must have degree exactly two, so the degree sum is 2n and n edges remain after halving, minus one
Each new vertex joins the tree by one edge, and any extra edge would close a cycle
Removing any edge from a tree leaves it connected, so n-1 edges is the most a tree can keep
Trees must be drawn without crossing edges, and planar drawings limit edges to n-1 for n vertices

rubric: Connecting n vertices needs n-1 edges; more would form a cycle.
Removing a tree edge disconnects it, so the last option is false.

items.prompt: What does it mean for a graph to be connected?

options.label: Every vertex is adjacent to every other vertex
Every vertex has degree at least one
There is a path between every pair of vertices
The graph contains at least one cycle

rubric: Connected means a path exists between any two vertices.
Adjacency of all pairs is a complete graph; degree at least one does not ensure connection.

items.prompt: Which graph is bipartite?

options.label: A cycle on 4 vertices
A complete graph on 4 vertices
A cycle on 5 vertices
A triangle

rubric: Even cycles can be 2-colored, so they are bipartite.
Odd cycles and complete graphs on 3+ vertices contain odd cycles.

items.prompt: What is a matching in a graph?

options.label: A set of edges with no two sharing a vertex
A set of edges forming a closed path
A set of vertices that are all adjacent
A set of edges that touches every vertex at least twice

rubric: A matching has pairwise vertex-disjoint edges.
Closed paths are cycles; the other options misdescribe cliques or covers.

items.prompt: Which statements about a triangle (cycle on 3 vertices) are true? Select all that apply.

options.label: It is connected
Every vertex has degree 2
It can be properly colored with 2 colors
It is a tree

items.prompt: A school must schedule exams so that no two courses sharing a student are at the same time. A planner models courses as vertices and joins two courses if they share a student. What does a proper coloring of this graph give?

options.label: The shortest chain of courses linking any two students
A spanning tree connecting every course to one exam room
A matching that pairs each student with a single course
A conflict-free assignment of time slots to courses

rubric: Colors represent time slots; adjacent courses get different ones.
Paths, matchings and spanning trees answer different questions.

items.prompt: The sum of all vertex degrees in a simple graph is always equal to which quantity?

options.label: The number of vertices minus one, as in every connected graph
Twice the number of edges, since each edge adds 1 to two vertices
The number of edges, since each edge is counted once overall
The number of vertices times the number of edges in the graph

rubric: Each edge has two endpoints, so it contributes 2 to the degree sum (handshake lemma).
Distractors confuse the degree sum with the edge count or with tree facts.

items.prompt: A tree has 10 vertices. How many edges does it have?
rubric: Every tree with n vertices has n-1 edges, so 9.
10 is a common slip equating edges with vertices; 45 is the edge count of the complete graph.

items.prompt: Which statement correctly describes a tree?

options.label: A graph in which every vertex has exactly two neighbours
A connected graph in which every edge lies on some cycle
A graph with no cycles, which is allowed to be disconnected
A connected graph that contains no cycles at all

rubric: A tree is a connected acyclic graph.
Allowing disconnection describes a forest; degree 2 everywhere describes cycles.

items.prompt: Which of these graphs is bipartite?

options.label: A triangle (cycle on 3 vertices)
A cycle on 4 vertices
The complete graph on 4 vertices
A cycle on 5 vertices

rubric: A graph is bipartite exactly when it has no odd cycle; a 4-cycle is even and can be 2-coloured.
The 3- and 5-cycles are odd cycles, and K4 contains triangles.

items.prompt: In the standard definition used in graph theory, which statement describes a path between two vertices?

options.label: A walk that visits every vertex in the graph at least once
A walk in which no edge is used more than once, though vertices may repeat
A walk in which no vertex is repeated along the way
A walk that begins and ends at the same vertex

rubric: A path never repeats a vertex.
The first distractor describes a trail, the third a closed walk, the fourth a spanning walk.

items.prompt: Which of the following statements are true of every tree with at least 2 vertices (simple graphs)? Select all that apply.

options.label: Adding one new edge between two non-adjacent vertices creates exactly one cycle
There is exactly one path between any two vertices
Removing any single edge leaves the graph connected
It contains at least two vertices of degree 1
Every vertex has degree at least 2

rubric: Trees have unique paths, a unique cycle on adding an edge, and at least two leaves.
Removing a tree edge disconnects it, and leaves have degree 1, so the other two statements fail.

items.prompt: A company maps its computers as vertices and direct cables as edges. Machines in the office form one group linked together, and machines in the warehouse form another group linked together, but no cable joins the two groups. What does this say about the graph?

options.label: It is disconnected, with two connected components
It is a tree, because each group is linked internally
It contains an Euler circuit, since no cable joins the two groups
It is connected, because every machine has at least one cable

rubric: No path between the groups means the graph is disconnected with two components.
Having degree at least 1 everywhere does not imply connectivity.

items.prompt: A graph has 7 edges. What is the sum of the degrees of all its vertices?
rubric: Degree sum is twice the edge count: 14.
7 counts each edge once; the others apply wrong multipliers.

items.prompt: A connected simple graph on 5 vertices has one of these degree lists. Which one guarantees an Euler circuit?
rubric: A connected graph has an Euler circuit exactly when every degree is even.
Each other list contains odd degrees.

items.prompt: What is the minimum number of colours needed to properly colour the vertices of a cycle on 5 vertices?
rubric: An odd cycle is not bipartite, so 2 colours fail, but 3 suffice.
Choosing 2 comes from assuming all cycles are bipartite.

items.prompt: A graph has adjacency lists: A: B, C; B: A, D; C: A, E; D: B, E; E: C, D. What is the length, in edges, of a shortest path from A to E?
rubric: A-C-E uses 2 edges, and A has no direct edge to E.
3 comes from taking A-B-D-E, a longer route.

items.prompt: How many edges does the complete graph on 6 vertices have?
rubric: K6 has 6*5/2 = 15 edges.
30 forgets to halve the ordered pairs; 36 is 6 squared.

items.prompt: Each list gives the vertex degrees of a connected graph. Which graphs must have an Euler path (a trail using every edge once)? Select all that apply.
rubric: A connected graph has an Euler path when it has 0 or 2 odd-degree vertices.
The last two lists have four odd vertices each.

items.prompt: A school schedules exams in time slots. Courses A, B and C each share students with each other, and course D shares students only with A. Two courses sharing students cannot be in the same slot. Modelling courses as vertices and conflicts as edges, what is the fewest slots needed?

options.label: 4 slots, because D conflicts with A so it needs a fourth slot of its own
2 slots, because the graph is a triangle with one pendant vertex, so two colours alternate
2 slots, because the longest path in the graph has just four vertices
3 slots, because A, B and C form a triangle and D can reuse B's slot

rubric: The triangle forces 3 colours, and D adjacent only to A can share a slot with B or C.
Assuming one slot per course ignores that non-adjacent vertices can share colours.

items.prompt: A simple 3-regular graph (every vertex has degree 3) has 10 vertices. How many edges does it have?
rubric: The degree sum is 10*3=30 and equals twice the edge count, so there are 15 edges.
30 forgets to halve the degree sum; 10 confuses vertex count with edge count.

items.prompt: A forest (an acyclic graph) has 12 vertices and 3 connected components. How many edges does it have?
rubric: Each tree component has one fewer edge than vertices, so the total is 12-3=9.
11 applies the single-tree formula n-1 to the whole forest.

items.prompt: A graph has edges A-B, A-C, B-D, C-D and D-E. Running depth-first search from A, always visiting the alphabetically smallest unvisited neighbour first, what is the visit order?

options.label: A, B, D, C, E
A, B, D, E, C
A, C, D, B, E
A, B, C, D, E

rubric: DFS goes A, B, D, then at D takes C before E, and finally backtracks to D to visit E.
A, B, C, D, E is the breadth-first order.

items.prompt: What is the chromatic number of the cycle graph C7 (a single cycle on 7 vertices)?
rubric: Odd cycles are not bipartite, so 2 colours fail, but 3 colours suffice.
2 is the answer for even cycles only.

items.prompt: A weighted graph on vertices A to E has edges AB=4, AC=2, BC=1, BD=5, CD=8, CE=10, DE=2. What is the total weight of a minimum spanning tree?
rubric: Kruskal takes BC=1, AC=2, DE=2, skips AB (cycle), then takes BD=5, giving 10.
14 comes from including AB and skipping the cheaper DE or similar errors; 12 comes from using CD or CE badly.

items.prompt: Which of these graphs have an Euler circuit (a closed walk using every edge exactly once)? Select all that apply.

options.label: C6, the cycle on 6 vertices
K4, the complete graph on 4 vertices
K3,3, the complete bipartite graph with parts of size 3
K5, the complete graph on 5 vertices
P4, the path on 4 vertices

rubric: A connected graph has an Euler circuit exactly when every vertex has even degree: K5 has degree 4 and C6 has degree 2.
K4 and K3,3 have degree 3 everywhere, and P4 has two odd-degree endpoints.

items.prompt: A delivery network has a depot S and stops A, B, C. Two-way road lengths are S-A 2, S-B 5, A-B 1, A-C 7 and B-C 3. A dispatcher runs Dijkstra's algorithm from S. What distance does it report for C?
rubric: The best route is S-A-B-C with length 2+1+3=6.
8 is the route S-B-C and 9 is S-A-C, which skip the cheaper detour through A and B.

items.prompt: Someone claims a simple graph on 4 vertices can have degrees 3, 3, 3, 1, since the degree sum 10 is even. Why is no such graph possible?

options.label: The handshake lemma requires the number of vertices of odd degree to be odd, but this sequence has four of them.
Each degree-3 vertex must be adjacent to all others, so the fourth vertex would also have degree 3.
A vertex of degree 1 is only allowed in trees, and three degree-3 vertices would form a cycle.
A graph on four vertices has at most three edges, but this sequence would need five edges in total.

rubric: Degree 3 on 4 vertices means adjacent to every other vertex, which forces the last vertex to have degree 3, not 1.
The parity check passes (10 is even), so the handshake lemma alone does not rule it out; the edge maximum is 6, not 3.

items.prompt: A DFS-based cycle detector for undirected graphs reports a cycle on a plain tree. It flags a cycle whenever it meets an already visited neighbour. What is the cause?

options.label: It treats the edge back to the vertex's parent as a back edge, so the tree edge just used looks like a cycle.
It marks vertices as visited only after exploring all their neighbours, so some edges are met twice and look like repeats.
It starts the search from a single root vertex, so edges in other components are skipped and later reached from both ends.
It uses recursion rather than an explicit stack, so a vertex on the call stack is wrongly treated as already finished.

rubric: In an undirected graph every tree edge is seen again from the child, so the parent must be excluded when checking visited neighbours.
The other options misattribute the bug to direction or traversal type.

items.prompt: A connected graph has 10 vertices and 13 edges. What is the minimum number of edges to remove so that it becomes a tree (still connected, no cycles)?
rubric: A spanning tree has 9 edges, so 13-9=4 edges must be removed, each breaking a cycle.
3 subtracts 10 from 13 and 9 confuses the tree's edge count with the removals.

items.prompt: A greedy colouring algorithm uses 3 colours on a graph known to be bipartite. What does this show?

options.label: Greedy colouring gives the minimum number of colours here, so the chromatic number is 3 and the bipartite claim is wrong.
The graph is not bipartite, since a correct colouring algorithm should not need more colours than the chromatic number.
The result depends on vertex order; another order would use 2 colours, so the chromatic number is still 2.
The graph has an odd cycle, because a proper colouring with 3 colours indicates that one exists in the graph.

rubric: Greedy colouring is order-dependent and can exceed the chromatic number; bipartite graphs always have a 2-colouring.
The distractors wrongly assume greedy colouring is optimal.

items.prompt: Applicants P1, P2, P3 can each do jobs {a, b}, and applicant P4 can do only job c. Why can't all four applicants be matched to distinct jobs?

options.label: There are four applicants but only three distinct jobs overall, so a full matching is impossible by counting.
P4 has just one acceptable job, which is fewer than the other applicants have, so Hall's condition fails.
P1, P2 and P3 together have only two available jobs, a and b, so Hall's condition fails for that set.
Job c is listed only once, while jobs a and b are each listed three times, which breaks the matching.

rubric: Three applicants whose combined neighbourhood is only {a, b} violates Hall's condition, so at most 3 can be matched.
Having one option (P4) is no obstacle by itself, and there are exactly three jobs but listing counts are irrelevant.

items.prompt: Two triangles share exactly one vertex v (a bowtie graph, 5 vertices and 6 edges). Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.label: The graph needs 4 colours.
The graph is bipartite.
The graph has an Euler circuit.
Vertex v is a cut vertex.
The graph has a bridge.

rubric: Removing v disconnects the triangles, and all degrees are even (v has 4, others 2), so an Euler circuit exists.
Every edge lies on a triangle so there is no bridge; triangles make it non-bipartite, and 3 colours suffice.

items.prompt: A routing tool runs Dijkstra from S on a directed graph with edges S→A 2, S→B 3, B→A -2 and A→C 4. It reports distance 6 to C, yet the path S→B→A→C costs only 5. What is the cause?

options.label: The edge A→C is too long for the priority queue to compare, so the tool kept the first distance it found to C.
Directed graphs need a separate algorithm for every vertex, so the tool must have handled the edge direction wrongly.
Dijkstra picks B before A because B is nearer to S, so the update of A through B is skipped by its tie-breaking rule when distances are compared.
Dijkstra finalizes A at distance 2 and never revisits it, which fails with a negative edge.

rubric: Dijkstra's greedy finalization relies on non-negative weights; the negative edge B→A makes the finalized value for A wrong.
B is not picked before A (2 < 3), and direction or queue size are unrelated to the failure.

items.prompt: A graph has 8 vertices and 7 edges, and it contains a cycle. Which conclusion must hold?

options.label: It is connected, since 7 edges are enough to join 8 vertices through the cycle
It is disconnected, since a connected graph with 7 edges on 8 vertices is acyclic
It has an isolated vertex, since the cycle uses up too many of the edges
It is a tree, since 8 vertices with 7 edges always form a tree shape

rubric: A connected graph on n vertices with n-1 edges is a tree and has no cycle, so this graph must be disconnected.
Distractors confuse edge count alone with being a tree, or assume an isolated vertex is forced.

items.prompt: Which statement about a closed walk of odd length in a graph is correct?

options.label: It guarantees a triangle, because the shortest possible odd closed walk has length 3 and must be a triangle
It is itself a cycle, because every closed walk returns to its start vertex without repeating any edge
It guarantees nothing, because walks may repeat edges and so odd closed walks occur in bipartite graphs
It guarantees an odd cycle, because splitting at a repeated vertex gives shorter closed walks, one odd

rubric: Splitting an odd closed walk at a repeated vertex yields two shorter closed walks, one of which is odd, so an odd cycle exists.
Distractors treat walks as cycles, force triangles, or wrongly allow odd closed walks in bipartite graphs.

items.prompt: Each sequence below has an even sum and 5 terms. Which one is NOT the degree sequence of any simple graph?
rubric: Three vertices of degree 4 on 5 vertices are adjacent to everything, so every vertex has degree at least 3, contradicting the 1s.
An even sum is necessary but not sufficient; the other sequences can be realised.

items.prompt: Dijkstra's algorithm returns a wrong distance on a graph containing one negative edge weight (no negative cycle). What is the precise reason?

options.label: A negative edge creates a negative cycle, so shortest paths are not well defined here
Relaxation is valid only for positive totals, so it skips edges that would lower a distance
A vertex is finalised when popped, but a negative edge can later shorten its distance
The priority queue is unable to hold negative keys, so the extraction order is undefined

rubric: Dijkstra assumes a finalised vertex cannot be improved, which fails when a later negative edge lowers the path cost.
Distractors blame data structures or wrongly claim a negative edge implies a negative cycle.

items.prompt: A connected graph has exactly 4 vertices of odd degree. What is the fewest trails, sharing no edges, that together use every edge exactly once?
rubric: Each trail has two odd-degree endpoints at most, so 4 odd vertices need at least 2 trails, and 2 suffice.
Answer 1 mistakes this for an Euler trail, which allows only 0 or 2 odd vertices.

items.prompt: Which statements about minimum spanning trees (MSTs) of a connected weighted graph are true? Select all that apply.

options.label: If all edge weights are distinct, the MST is unique
Deleting any edge of an MST leaves the remaining edges still connected
The MST path between two vertices is always a shortest path in the graph
An edge strictly heavier than all other edges on some cycle is in no MST

rubric: Distinct weights force a unique MST, and the strictly heaviest edge on a cycle is excluded by the cycle property.
MST paths minimise total tree weight, not path length, and removing a tree edge disconnects the tree.

items.prompt: During a DFS of a connected undirected graph, vertex v is not the root and has a tree child c. No back edge from c's subtree reaches a proper ancestor of v, but one reaches v itself, so low[c] = disc[v]. What follows?

options.label: v is not an articulation point, but the tree edge v–c is a bridge
v is not an articulation point, and the tree edge v–c is not a bridge
v is an articulation point, and the tree edge v–c is a bridge
v is an articulation point, but the tree edge v–c is not a bridge

rubric: The articulation condition is low[c] >= disc[v], while a bridge needs the strict low[c] > disc[v].
Distractors mix up the two conditions, treating the equality case as a bridge or as harmless.

items.prompt: A graph has 1,000,000 vertices and about 5,000,000 edges. The main task is a BFS that iterates over each vertex's neighbours, and memory is limited. Which representation best meets these criteria?

options.label: Bit-packed adjacency matrix, because packing removes any pointer overhead entirely
Adjacency list, because storage grows with V + E and iteration costs only each degree
Unsorted edge list, because it stores each edge once and can be scanned quickly
Adjacency matrix, because constant-time edge lookup is what the BFS needs most

rubric: A sparse graph suits adjacency lists: O(V+E) memory and neighbour iteration proportional to degree.
A matrix needs V^2 entries, and an edge list makes finding a vertex's neighbours slow.

items.prompt: A student claims: 'Every graph with maximum degree 3 can be properly coloured with 3 colours, since greedy colouring never needs more than the maximum degree.' Which critique is most accurate?

options.label: The claim fails only for bipartite graphs, since they need 2 colours and greedy may then exceed 3
The claim fails for every graph with a cycle, since cycles force more colours than the maximum degree
Greedy guarantees only Δ+1 colours; K4 has Δ = 3 yet needs 4, so the claim fails for complete graphs
The claim is correct, since each vertex has at most 3 neighbours and so always has a free colour

rubric: Greedy gives at most Δ+1 colours; K4 is a counterexample, and Brooks' theorem excludes only complete graphs and odd cycles.
Distractors ignore the Δ+1 bound or invent failures for bipartite or cyclic graphs.

items.prompt: You need an MST of a weighted graph with 2,000 vertices and nearly every possible edge present, stored as an adjacency matrix. You want the best worst-case time with simple code. Which choice is best?

options.label: Kruskal with full sorting, since O(E log E) is competitive and the union-find step adds little cost
Prim with a binary heap, since O(E log V) grows more slowly than O(V^2) once the graph has many edges
Dijkstra from one vertex, since the shortest-path tree it builds is a minimum spanning tree when weights are positive
Prim with an array scan, since O(V^2) matches the dense input and needs no heap

rubric: On dense graphs E is near V^2, so array-based Prim at O(V^2) beats heap-based O(E log V) and Kruskal's sorting.
Distractors apply heap or sorting advantages that hold only for sparse graphs, or confuse shortest-path trees with MSTs.

items.prompt: A proof claims: 'In a bipartite graph, repeatedly pick any edge and delete both endpoints; the final set of picked edges is a maximum matching, since nothing more can be added.' What is the flaw?

options.label: 'Nothing more can be added' shows only a maximal matching; on path a-b-c-d, picking b–c blocks a–b, c–d
The result is maximum only for trees, since cycles let the process pick two edges sharing a vertex
Bipartite graphs have no maximum matching unless Hall's condition holds, so the process never terminates
Deleting endpoints changes the bipartition, so later chosen edges no longer form a valid matching

rubric: Greedy yields a maximal matching, which can be smaller than a maximum one, as the 4-vertex path shows.
Distractors misstate Hall's condition or claim the process produces invalid matchings.

items.prompt: You must schedule exams into the fewest time slots so no student sits two exams in one slot. Which model and target best fit this goal?

options.label: Vertices are time slots, edges join slots sharing a student; find a spanning tree
Vertices are exams, edges join exams sharing a student; find the chromatic number
Vertices are students, edges join students sharing an exam; find the chromatic number
Vertices are exams, edges join exams sharing a student; find a maximum matching

rubric: Slots are colours, and conflicting exams must get different colours, so the minimum slots equal the chromatic number of the exam-conflict graph.
Distractors model the wrong objects or use a matching or tree, which does not capture conflict-free grouping.

items.prompt: Which arguments validly show that a given connected graph is NOT bipartite? Select all that apply.

options.label: Show the graph has an odd number of vertices
Show that some vertex has odd degree
Run BFS and find an edge joining two vertices on the same level
Exhibit one cycle of odd length in the graph
Exhibit a closed walk of odd length

rubric: Odd cycles, same-level BFS edges and odd closed walks each imply an odd cycle, which rules out bipartiteness.
Odd vertex count or odd degree is irrelevant: a path on 3 vertices is bipartite and has both.

items.prompt: A city must plough every street segment at least once, starting and ending at the depot. The street graph is connected and every intersection has an even number of segments. The planner wants the cheapest correct method.

options.label: Solve a travelling salesman tour, since the route must start and end at the depot intersection
Find a Hamiltonian cycle, since visiting every intersection exactly once will also cover every street
Compute a minimum spanning tree, since it joins all intersections with the least total street length
Find an Euler circuit, since all-even degrees guarantee a closed route using each segment exactly once

rubric: Connected with all even degrees means an Euler circuit exists and can be found in linear time, covering each street once.
Hamiltonian and TSP formulations target vertices, not edges, and are far costlier; an MST omits streets.

items.prompt: A student proves that every finite graph with minimum degree at least 2 contains a cycle: take a longest path v1...vk; v1 has a neighbour other than v2, which must lie on the path by maximality, closing a cycle. How should this proof be judged?

options.label: Valid: maximality forces every neighbour of v1 onto the path, and one other than v2 closes a cycle of length at least 3.
Flawed: the only other neighbour of v1 could be v2 itself, so no cycle is guaranteed and the argument really needs minimum degree at least 3.
Valid only for a tree plus one edge, since a longest path needs a unique endpoint to be well defined in the argument.
Flawed: a longest path may not exist when the graph is disconnected, so the argument only covers connected graphs with a single component.

rubric: Maximality of the path puts all of v1's neighbours on it, and degree at least 2 gives one besides v2, so a cycle exists.
Distractors target confusion about v2 being the only neighbour and about disconnected graphs; the path lies inside one component, so that is harmless.

items.prompt: A report states: 'By Brooks' theorem, every connected graph with maximum degree D can be properly coloured with D colours.' How should the claim be judged?

options.label: Wrong: graphs containing a triangle need more than D colours, and Brooks' theorem guarantees D colours just for triangle-free connected graphs.
Wrong: complete graphs and odd cycles need D+1 colours, and Brooks' theorem exists precisely to exclude those two families.
Right: Brooks' theorem gives D colours for connected graphs, and its exceptions arise for disconnected inputs with several components.
Right: greedy colouring in a suitable vertex order needs at most D colours, because each vertex has at most D neighbours to avoid.

rubric: K_{D+1} and odd cycles are connected and need D+1 colours; Brooks' theorem states they are the only exceptions.
Greedy colouring only guarantees D+1 colours, which is the misconception behind the first option.

items.prompt: In a bipartite graph with sides A and B, every vertex of A has degree at least k (k >= 1) and every vertex of B has degree at most k. Which judgement about matchings is correct?

options.label: A matching covering A need not exist, since Hall's condition needs |A| = |B| and the degree bounds do not force that.
A matching covering A exists: at least k|S| edges leave S and each vertex of N(S) takes at most k, so |N(S)| >= |S|.
A matching covering A exists only when every vertex of B also has degree exactly k, so that edges and vertices balance.
A matching covering A is not guaranteed, since two A-vertices of degree k may share all neighbours and so violate Hall's condition.

rubric: Counting edges out of any S in A gives Hall's condition, so an A-saturating matching exists.
The sharing counterexample violates the bound on B-degrees, and the sides need not be equal.

items.prompt: A team must compute a minimum spanning tree of a graph with 4,000 vertices and about 7.9 million edges (nearly complete), stored as an adjacency matrix. Judged on running time, which algorithm is best?

options.label: Kruskal with sorted edges, O(E log E) or about 180 million steps, since sorting gives the same guarantee at any density.
Prim with a binary heap, O(E log V), since a heap is always at least as fast as scanning an array of keys.
Prim with an array scan, O(V^2) or about 16 million steps, which beats edge-based methods on near-complete graphs.
Dijkstra from one vertex, O(V^2), since its shortest-path tree is a minimum spanning tree whenever weights are distinct.

rubric: On dense graphs O(V^2) beats O(E log V) and O(E log E) because E is close to V^2.
Distractors assume heaps or sorting are always better, or confuse shortest-path trees with minimum spanning trees.

items.prompt: A ten-site network must keep every site reachable after the failure of any single link, using as few links as possible. Which topology best meets both criteria?

options.label: A spanning tree plus one extra link joining two nearby sites: 10 links, but the tree's other links stay bridges and their failure splits the network.
One cycle through all ten sites: 10 links and no bridge, so any single failure still leaves a path between every pair.
A complete graph on the ten sites: 45 links, the only layout in which no single link failure can disconnect any site from the others.
A star around one hub: 9 links, since every site is one hop from the hub and a link failure cuts only one leaf.

rubric: Surviving any link failure needs no bridges, which requires at least n edges; a Hamiltonian cycle meets this with exactly n.
A tree plus one edge still has bridges outside its single cycle, and a star has 9 bridges.

items.prompt: Which claims about graph colouring are correct? Select all that apply.

options.label: A graph with chromatic number k must contain a clique of size k, since the colours need pairwise adjacent vertices.
Every planar graph can be properly coloured with 4 colours, by the Four Colour Theorem.
For n vertices, the chromatic number is at least n divided by the size of a largest independent set.
A graph with no K4 subgraph can always be coloured with 3 colours, since cliques force the colour counts.

rubric: Colour classes are independent sets, so at least n/alpha colours are needed; planar graphs are 4-colourable.
Triangle-free graphs with large chromatic number (Mycielski) refute the clique-based claims.

items.prompt: An exam timetabling team models courses as vertices, joining two when students sit both. A greedy colouring gives 7 time slots. A colleague separately finds 5 courses that pairwise share students. The team lead says: 'Seven slots is provably optimal.' How should this be judged?

options.label: Unsupported, but the optimum must be exactly 5, because a clique of size 5 fixes the chromatic number of the whole graph.
Unsupported: the clique only bounds the answer from above and greedy bounds it from below, so 5 to 7 slots are possible.
Unsupported: the clique gives a lower bound of 5, greedy gives an upper bound of 7, so the optimum may be 5, 6 or 7.
Correct: greedy colourings are optimal whenever the graph contains a clique, so seven slots is the minimum possible number.

rubric: A clique gives a lower bound and a greedy colouring an upper bound, so the optimum lies between 5 and 7 and 7 is unproven.
Distractors swap the bounds or treat a clique or greedy result as determining the exact value.

items.prompt: In a directed graph with nonnegative weights you need the cheapest path from s to t using at most k edges, though the cheapest unrestricted path may use many more. Which design is correct?

options.label: Run Dijkstra, delete the edges of the shortest path found, and repeat k times, taking the cheapest of the results.
Run Dijkstra from s, stop once k vertices have been finalised, then read off the cost to t from the stored distances.
Add a large constant to every weight to penalise long paths, then run Dijkstra once from s and read the cost to t.
Run k rounds of edge relaxation, keeping the best cost per vertex using at most i edges, for O(k*E) time overall.

rubric: A layered Bellman-Ford style DP on (vertex, edges used) enforces the edge limit exactly.
Dijkstra's finalisation order is by cost, not edge count, and weight shifting changes which path is cheapest.

items.prompt: A bipartite conflict graph with 100,000 vertices needs a smallest set of vertices touching every edge (a minimum vertex cover), computed exactly in polynomial time. Which design meets this?

options.label: Take both endpoints of every edge in a maximal matching, which yields a minimum cover on bipartite graphs by a counting argument.
Find a maximum matching with Hopcroft-Karp, then build the cover from alternating-path reachability using Konig's theorem.
Treat it as general vertex cover and use exhaustive search, since no exact polynomial method exists even for bipartite graphs.
Repeatedly pick the vertex of highest remaining degree and delete it, which is exact on bipartite graphs because of their structure.

rubric: Konig's theorem equates minimum vertex cover and maximum matching sizes in bipartite graphs and gives a constructive cover.
Greedy and maximal-matching methods are only approximations; bipartite vertex cover is not NP-hard.

items.prompt: You must construct a graph that contains no triangle but cannot be properly coloured with fewer than 4 colours. Which construction works?

options.label: Join a new vertex to every vertex of the 5-cycle, producing the 6-vertex wheel on a rim of five.
Apply the Mycielski construction to the 5-cycle, which yields the 11-vertex Grotzsch graph.
Take the Petersen graph, which has girth 5 and so should need four colours once its odd cycles are counted.
Subdivide every edge of K4 once, so that each original edge becomes a path with two edges.

rubric: The Mycielskian of a triangle-free graph is triangle-free and has chromatic number one higher; C5 has 3, so the result has 4.
The Petersen graph is 3-colourable, the wheel contains triangles, and subdivided K4 is bipartite.

items.prompt: A connected road network has exactly 4 odd-degree junctions. An inspector must walk a closed route covering every road at least once with minimum total length. Which plan meets this?

options.label: Pair the odd junctions to minimise total shortest-path distance, duplicate those paths, then walk an Euler circuit.
Skip the cheapest road at each odd junction so that all degrees become even, then walk the resulting Euler circuit.
Duplicate the single cheapest road at each odd junction, then walk an Euler circuit of the enlarged network of roads.
Build a minimum spanning tree over all junctions, then walk each tree road twice, once in each direction, to close the route.

rubric: The route inspection solution adds a minimum-weight pairing of odd vertices via shortest paths, making all degrees even.
Distractors duplicate locally cheap roads that may not fix parity, or drop roads that must be covered.

items.prompt: A proposed bridge-finding DFS sets low[v] = min(disc[v], low[w] for tree children w, disc[w] for every neighbour w of v) and flags tree edge (u,v) as a bridge when low[v] > disc[u]. What is the design missing?

options.label: It must skip the tree edge back to v's parent, identified by edge id, or every tree edge appears to lie on a cycle.
It must sort adjacency lists by degree first, since the bridge test depends on visiting low-degree neighbours before others.
It must use the test low[v] >= disc[u], since the strict inequality misses bridges whose upper endpoint is the root of the search.
It must run a second DFS on the reversed graph, because low values from a single traversal order undercount the cycles.

rubric: Without excluding the parent edge, low[v] <= disc[u] always holds, so no bridge is ever reported; using edge ids also handles parallel edges.
The >= test is for articulation points, and traversal order does not affect correctness.

items.prompt: A design must be a connected simple graph on exactly 7 vertices that has an Euler trail but no Euler circuit. Which candidates meet every constraint? Select all that apply.

options.label: The path on 7 vertices
The star with 6 leaves
The wheel with a hub and 6 rim vertices
The complete graph K7
The complete bipartite graph K(2,5)

rubric: An Euler trail without a circuit needs exactly two odd-degree vertices: the path has two, and K(2,5) has two of degree 5.
K7 has all degrees even, while the star and the wheel each have six odd vertices.

items.prompt: A league organiser has 6 teams and needs a round-robin lasting exactly 5 rounds. Every pair must meet exactly once, and each team must play exactly one match in every round. Which scheduling design satisfies all of these constraints?

options.label: Alternate the edges of one Hamiltonian cycle as two rounds, then repeat those two rounds until every pair has met once.
Fix one team and place the other five on a cycle; each round pair the fixed team with one, mirror the rest, then rotate.
Colour the edges of K6 with first-fit greedy colouring and use the colour classes as rounds, accepting however many result.
Each round, greedily choose any unplayed pairs among teams not yet scheduled that round, continuing until the round is full.

rubric: The circle method decomposes K6 into 5 perfect matchings, giving exactly 5 valid rounds.
Greedy choices can get stuck or exceed 5 rounds, and repeating cycle edges rematches the same pairs.
